title: Faster Than Ninja
excerpt: Posted on 5 Aug 2026 by Boris Kolpackov
content_html:
Posted on 5 Aug 2026 by Boris Kolpackov

Some months ago I read an article about a tool for snooping on slow build systems that can be used to find build bottlenecks. While the whole article is quite illuminating, this quote stood out to me:

Ninja is not a 100% fair comparison to other tools, because it benefits from some "baked in" build logic by the tool that created the ninja file, but I think it's a reasonable "speed of light" performance benchmark for build systems.

To clarify, by "baked in" the author means that nobody writes Ninja build files by hand. Rather, a second tool, such as CMake, is invoked to generate them and some steps performed during this generation phase (examples below) should ideally be part of the build phase. Also, Ninja is notoriously minimalist, providing only the bare minimum of functionality, especially on the change tracking side of things (again, examples below). A modern build system would be expected to provide more.

Still, it would be interesting to see how close a modern, native (that is, without the generation step) build system can approach the "speed of light".

Let's take a look at how build2 measures up. While there is a number of substantial projects (such as Boost and Qt) that can be built with both build systems, finding a project of substance that would result in an apples-to-apples comparison is difficult because when we package more complex projects for build2, we invariably have to untangle the "ball of intra-dependencies" structure into something more orderly (for a good example, take a look at the upstream qtbase module versus build2 packages). And this usually results in a slightly different set of intermediate build artifacts, like bootstrap and utility libraries.

So we will have to make do with something simpler, where we can make sure the same set of object files and binaries is produced with more or less identical compile and link options. In the end I've picked Xerces-C++, an XML parser/serializer for C++. It has quite a few features (like XML Schema validation) so it's not exactly tiny, measuring 299 C++ translation units that are linked into a shared library.

We are going to test a full, from-scratch build, the same as in the quoted article. Ninja completes this build on my machine (see Benchmark Details below) in 3.4s:

Time (mean ± σ):    3.429 s ± 0.029 s  [User: 48.536s, System: 5.033s]
Range (min … max):  3.383 s … 3.464 s  10 runs

Before we measure build2, let's at least acknowledge the elephant in the room: while Ninja builds the project in 3.4s, CMake takes 15.6s to generate the Ninja build files. So if you had Xerces-C++ as a dependency of your project and it was being built from scratch, you would wait 19 seconds, not 3.4, for this build.

With the matching configuration (same C++ compiler, C++ standard, debug build, etc) build2 takes 3.8s, or about 11% slower:

Time (mean ± σ):    3.808 s ± 0.046 s  [User: 58.037s, System: 8.012s]
Range (min … max):  3.746 s … 3.886 s  10 runs

Pretty close, but not at the speed of light. Let's see if we can get there. Maybe building in vacuum will help?

To try to get closer to Ninja's time we are going to make the comparison more accurately apples-to-apples. As discussed above, Ninja is notoriously minimalist with build2 providing a lot of functionality that Ninja does not. And some of this functionality has measurable cost, performance-wise. So we are going to disable a few features to closer match the amount of work done by Ninja.

The first feature that we will disable is the more precise change tracking for C and C++ source files. Ninja simply checks whether the file's modification time has changed and if so, recompiles it. build2, in contrast, performs an extra step in this case: it tokenizes the (partially-preprocessed) source file and computes the checksum of the resulting tokens. If this checksum hasn't changed since the last time the file was compiled, then it skips recompiling it. This ignores whitespace-only changes (as long as they do not alter the column numbers of the tokens) and is very useful during development (and is critical in some case, like if you want to change your project's version with every commit). But tokenizing all the 299 translation units in the from-scratch build has an upfront cost, even if it may pay off during further incremental builds.

The way to disable this ignorable change detection is to tell build2 that the project is read-only (which is done automatically by the package manager for external dependencies). In this case build2 will fall back to using just the modification time, the same as Ninja. With this change our build time goes down to 3.4s, pretty much the same as Ninja's:

Time (mean ± σ):    3.433 s ± 0.055 s  [User: 51.093s, System: 6.701s]
Range (min … max):  3.383 s … 3.551 s  10 runs

Let's see if we can go even faster. Next, we disable compression in the file cache. We will discuss the file cache in more detail a bit later but for now let's just say that by disabling compression we trade temporary disk space usage for speed:

Time (mean ± σ):    3.355 s ± 0.067 s  [User: 49.987s, System: 6.153s]
Range (min … max):  3.281 s … 3.471 s  10 runs

And now we are 2.2% faster than Ninja! While this may not seem like much, it becomes more impressive considering build2 still does a lot more than Ninja. Some of this work is done by CMake and some is just not done at all.

For example, build2 generates the XercesVersion.hpp header from XercesVersion.hpp.in as part of the build while Ninja leaves this to CMake. build2 also makes sure this file is properly change-tracked (while Ninja expects you to re-run CMake manually). This header is included in pretty much every translation unit in Xerces-C++, meaning that no compilation can start until it is generated. As an experiment, I hacked the build2 build file to pretend XercesVersion.hpp is static. That increased the gap to 2.6%.

build2 also has to extract a lot more information from the compiler, something that in the case of Ninja is, again, done by CMake. Things like the compiler id (GCC, Clang, etc) and its version, target platform, list of system header and library search paths, C and C++ standard libraries used, etc. This information is both made available to build files as well as used to implement more precise change tracking. For example, for C and C++, besides tracking changes to the standard inputs such as the source file itself, all the included headers, and the compile options, build2 also tracks the compiler id/version, system header search paths, and environment variables that may affect the compilation.

Currently, the only reliable way to extract this information is to run the compiler. And, unfortunately, to extract all the bits listed above, we have to run it multiple times. For example, in case of GCC, there are 10 invocations in total, 5 for C and 5 for C++ (Xerces-C++ has a few C translation units):

LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -v
gcc-15 -g -print-multiarch
gcc-15 -g -x c -E -
LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -std=c9x -print-search-dirs
LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -std=c9x -x c -v -E -

LC_ALL=C g++-15 -v
g++-15 -g -print-multiarch
g++-15 -g -x c++ -E -
LC_ALL=C g++-15 -std=gnu++17 -print-search-dirs
LC_ALL=C g++-15 -std=gnu++17 -x c++ -v -E -

Ok, so build2 does quite a bit more and is on par or even faster than Ninja, even when we choose not to see the elephant (CMake). The next natural question to ask is how does it do it? Ninja was designed from the start with performance in mind and then saw decades of heavy use and optimization. There is little chance of any fruit, let alone low-hanging ones, left for us to pick. So what's the secret?

In a nutshell, we have to do things differently, not just better. I can think of three major design decisions that contributed to this. It's not easy to verify empirically since it would be pretty difficult to test alternative designs in isolation, but I think they are the most likely reasons.

The first is more of a what not to do rather than what to do. Again, nothing will illustrate the point better than the above mentioned article:

Here’s a tiny slice of a CMake build from another open source project:

[...]

Here CMake gets Xcode’s path with xcode-select -print-path, the OS version with sw_vers, and then recursively calls cmake/make a few times for good measure, and finally compiles and links a file.

Only the green boxes in that timeline are doing useful work. One could argue that none of what CMake does is "useful work", in the sense that it just builds the thing that actually builds the project. Regardless, let’s just accept that CMake needs to do this weird cmake->make->make->clang dance to figure out the build environment.

Zooming out reveals that the weird dance happens 85 times!

Yikes, no parallelism. It also studiously re-checks the Xcode path and OS version 85 times, just in case the OS version changes mid-build.

Needless to say, you are not going to get very far performance-wise with such an approach. In contrast, in build2 we aggressively cache every piece of discovered information (but not across the build system runs) to make sure we don't redo any of the work unnecessarily.

Ok, I will stop picking on CMake and focus on Ninja. The second biggest difference between Ninja and build2 (the first being it's a native build system) is build2 being multi-threaded. While Ninja executes compilers, linkers, etc., in parallel, it performs its own housekeeping work serially, from a single thread. For example, both Ninja and build2 need to parse the header dependency information received from GCC, which is inconveniently produced as Makefile fragments. build2 does this (and a lot of other things) in parallel from multiple threads. In fact, the only serial phase in build2 is loading of build files (and even for that there are ideas on how to parallelize some parts of it).

The last design decision that I think contributes to build2 matching or exceeding Ninja's speed is a different C/C++ build model when it comes to the extraction of header dependency information (the list of headers included by every translation unit, transitively).

Ninja uses what we can call a byproduct of compilation model: during the from-scratch build, Ninja compiles every translation unit and gets the header dependency information essentially for free. It parses and stores it in its own format on disk to be used during the next build to see if any translation units need to be recompiled because some headers they include may have changed. This is a clever approach but unfortunately it doesn't work well with auto-generated headers (and is the reason why headers like XercesVersion.hpp are generated by CMake).

In build2 we perform explicit header dependency extraction before we compile a translation unit. One can reasonably expect a naive implementation to perform strictly worse than the byproduct approach, where this extraction is free. What we do in build2 is a bit more advanced: because a header dependency extraction is essentially a preprocessor run on the translation unit, we combine the dependency extraction with partial preprocessing of each translation unit. Or, in other words, instead of just extracting header dependencies, we perform partial preprocessing (-fdirective-only for GCC, -frewrite-includes for Clang) of each translation unit and get the header dependency information as a byproduct of that. Then, when the time comes to compile the translation unit, we compile this partially-preprocessed output instead of the original source file, thus saving on re-preprocessing it.

Remember the file cache compression that we disabled above? Well, that file cache is a temporary (unless C++20 modules are used) cache of the partially-preprocessed translation units.

Still, this sounds like a lot more work than what Ninja does. We even have to store the partially-preprocessed files on disk, how can this be faster than doing nothing? Interestingly, there appears to be another aspect at play: The way Ninja does it, preprocessing of translation units is spread out over the entire build, time-wise. There is also substantial demand for RAM since C and especially C++ compilation is memory-intensive. In contrast, with the build2 approach, all the preprocessing is front-loaded, it's all concentrated at the beginning of the build, before memory-intensive compilation starts. And preprocessing of a typical C/C++ translation unit involves including hundreds of header files (many of them the same as for other translation units), all of which need to be read from disk. It turns out, at least on Linux with GCC, the build2 approach performs better, likely due to better temporal locality of file access and lower memory pressure. In other words, with the build2 approach, the included headers are more likely to still sit in the system's file cache (for details, see Separate Preprocess and Compile Performance).

Benchmark Details

The benchmark was executed on a physical machine with Intel i9-12900K CPU running Debian on Samsung 980 Pro NVMe formatted as ext4. To obtain stable numbers I disabled turbo boost (failed that, the times gradually increased as the CPU got warmer):

echo 1 >/sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo

I used the official Xerces-C++ 3.3.0 source archive for Ninja and the libxerces-c-3.3.0+3 build2 package (which is the official source overlayed with build2 support). I had to modify CMakeLists.txt to change the hardcoded C++ standard from 14 to 17 since the system version of ICU on Debian no longer supports C++14.

The CMake command to prepare the Ninja build:

CC=gcc-15 CXX=g++-15 cmake -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -Dnetwork:BOOL=OFF \
  -Dtranscoder=icu \
  -Dmessage-loader=inmemory \
  -Dmutex-manager=standard \
  -Dxmlch-type=char16_t \
  ../xerces-c-3.3.0

Then to run the Ninja benchmark:

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'ninja clean' \
  'ninja src/all'

To run the build2 benchmark we don't need to prepare anything. Below are the command lines for the three measurements shown above:

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   xercesc/"

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   config.libxerces_c.build.readonly=true xercesc/"

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b --file-cache=none \
   config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   config.libxerces_c.build.readonly=true xercesc/"

blocks.html_en: To try to get closer to Ninja's time we are going to make the comparison more accurately apples-to-apples. As discussed above, Ninja is notoriously minimalist with build2 providing a lot of functionality that Ninja does not. And some of this functionality has measurable cost, performance-wise. So we are going to disable a few features to closer match the amount of work done by Ninja.

sentences.en: So we are going to disable a few features to closer match the amount of work done by Ninja.

blocks.html_en: The first feature that we will disable is the more precise change tracking for C and C++ source files. Ninja simply checks whether the file's modification time has changed and if so, recompiles it. build2, in contrast, performs an extra step in this case: it tokenizes the (partially-preprocessed) source file and computes the checksum of the resulting tokens. If this checksum hasn't changed since the last time the file was compiled, then it skips recompiling it. This ignores whitespace-only changes (as long as they do not alter the column numbers of the tokens) and is very useful during development (and is critical in some case, like if you want to change your project's version with every commit). But tokenizing all the 299 translation units in the from-scratch build has an upfront cost, even if it may pay off during further incremental builds.

blocks.html_en: Ok, I will stop picking on CMake and focus on Ninja. The second biggest difference between Ninja and build2 (the first being it's a native build system) is build2 being multi-threaded. While Ninja executes compilers, linkers, etc., in parallel, it performs its own housekeeping work serially, from a single thread. For example, both Ninja and build2 need to parse the header dependency information received from GCC, which is inconveniently produced as Makefile fragments. build2 does this (and a lot of other things) in parallel from multiple threads. In fact, the only serial phase in build2 is loading of build files (and even for that there are ideas on how to parallelize some parts of it).

sentences.zh: 好吧，我将不再选择 CMake，而专注于 Ninja。

sentences.en: The second biggest difference between Ninja and build2 (the first being it's a native build system) is build2 being multi-threaded.
sentences.zh: Ninja 和 build2 之间的第二个最大区别（第一个是它是本机构建系统）是 build2 是多线程的。

sentences.en: While Ninja executes compilers, linkers, etc., in parallel, it performs its own housekeeping work serially, from a single thread.
sentences.zh: 虽然 Ninja 并行执行编译器、链接器等，但它从单个线程串行执行自己的内务工作。

sentences.en: For example, both Ninja and build2 need to parse the header dependency information received from GCC, which is inconveniently produced as Makefile fragments.
sentences.zh: 例如，Ninja 和 build2 都需要解析从 GCC 接收到的头依赖信息，这些信息不方便地生成为 Makefile 片段。

sentences.en: build2 does this (and a lot of other things) in parallel from multiple threads.

blocks.html_en: The last design decision that I think contributes to build2 matching or exceeding Ninja's speed is a different C/C++ build model when it comes to the extraction of header dependency information (the list of headers included by every translation unit, transitively).

blocks.html_en: Ninja uses what we can call a byproduct of compilation model: during the from-scratch build, Ninja compiles every translation unit and gets the header dependency information essentially for free. It parses and stores it in its own format on disk to be used during the next build to see if any translation units need to be recompiled because some headers they include may have changed. This is a clever approach but unfortunately it doesn't work well with auto-generated headers (and is the reason why headers like XercesVersion.hpp are generated by CMake).

blocks.html_en: In build2 we perform explicit header dependency extraction before we compile a translation unit. One can reasonably expect a naive implementation to perform strictly worse than the byproduct approach, where this extraction is free. What we do in build2 is a bit more advanced: because a header dependency extraction is essentially a preprocessor run on the translation unit, we combine the dependency extraction with partial preprocessing of each translation unit. Or, in other words, instead of just extracting header dependencies, we perform partial preprocessing (-fdirective-only for GCC, -frewrite-includes for Clang) of each translation unit and get the header dependency information as a byproduct of that. Then, when the time comes to compile the translation unit, we compile this partially-preprocessed output instead of the original source file, thus saving on re-preprocessing it.

blocks.html_en: Still, this sounds like a lot more work than what Ninja does. We even have to store the partially-preprocessed files on disk, how can this be faster than doing nothing? Interestingly, there appears to be another aspect at play: The way Ninja does it, preprocessing of translation units is spread out over the entire build, time-wise. There is also substantial demand for RAM since C and especially C++ compilation is memory-intensive. In contrast, with the build2 approach, all the preprocessing is front-loaded, it's all concentrated at the beginning of the build, before memory-intensive compilation starts. And preprocessing of a typical C/C++ translation unit involves including hundreds of header files (many of them the same as for other translation units), all of which need to be read from disk. It turns out, at least on Linux with GCC, the build2 approach performs better, likely due to better temporal locality of file access and lower memory pressure. In other words, with the build2 approach, the included headers are more likely to still sit in the system's file cache (for details, see Separate Preprocess and Compile Performance).

content_html_zh:
发表于 2026 年 8 月 5 日，作者：鲍里斯·科尔帕科夫 (Boris Kolpackov)

几个月前，我读了一篇关于窥探缓慢构建系统的工具的文章，该工具可用于查找构建瓶颈。 虽然整篇文章都很有启发性，但下面这句话对我来说很突出：

Ninja 与其他工具的比较并不是 100% 公平，因为它受益于创建 ninja 文件的工具的一些“内置”构建逻辑，但我认为它是构建系统的合理“光速”性能基准。

澄清一下，作者所说的“烘焙”是指没有人手工编写 Ninja 构建文件。 相反，调用第二个工具（例如 CMake）来生成它们，并且在此生成阶段（下面的示例）期间执行的一些步骤理想情况下应该是构建阶段的一部分。 此外，Ninja 是出了名的极简主义，只提供最低限度的功能，特别是在变更跟踪方面（同样，下面的示例）。 现代构建系统有望提供更多功能。

尽管如此，看看现代的本地（即没有生成步骤）构建系统能够多么接近“光速”还是很有趣的。

让我们看看 build2 的表现如何。 虽然有许多实质性项目（例如 Boost 和 Qt）可以使用这两种构建系统构建，但找到一个能够进行同类比较的实质性项目是很困难的，因为当我们为 build2 打包更复杂的项目时，我们总是必须将“内部依赖关系球”结构分解为更有序的结构（作为一个很好的例子，看看上游 qtbase 模块与 build2 包）。 这通常会导致一组略有不同的中间构建工件，例如引导程序和实用程序库。

因此，我们将不得不使用更简单的方法，这样我们就可以确保使用或多或少相同的编译和链接选项生成相同的目标文件和二进制文件集。 最后我选择了 Xerces-C++，一个用于 C++ 的 XML 解析器/序列化器。 它具有相当多的功能（例如 XML 模式验证），因此它并不小，测量了链接到共享库的 299 个 C++ 翻译单元。

我们将测试一个完整的、从头开始的构建，与引用的文章中相同。 Ninja 在 3.4 秒内在我的机器上完成了此构建（请参阅下面的基准详细信息）：

Time (mean ± σ):    3.429 s ± 0.029 s  [User: 48.536s, System: 5.033s]
Range (min … max):  3.383 s … 3.464 s  10 runs

在我们测量 build2 之前，我们至少要承认房间里的大象：Ninja 在 3.4 秒内构建项目，而 CMake 需要 15.6 秒才能生成 Ninja 构建文件。 因此，如果您将 Xerces-C++ 作为项目的依赖项，并且它是从头开始构建的，则此构建将等待 19 秒，而不是 3.4 秒。

使用匹配的配置（相同的 C++ 编译器、C++ 标准、调试构建等），build2 需要 3.8 秒，或者慢大约 11%：

Time (mean ± σ):    3.808 s ± 0.046 s  [User: 58.037s, System: 8.012s]
Range (min … max):  3.746 s … 3.886 s  10 runs

非常接近，但不是光速。 让我们看看我们能否到达那里。 也许在真空中建造会有帮助？

为了更接近 Ninja 的时代，我们将进行更准确的同类比较。 如上所述，Ninja 是出了名的极简主义，build2 提供了许多 Ninja 没有的功能。 其中一些功能在性能方面具有可衡量的成本。 因此，我们将禁用一些功能，以更接近 Ninja 所做的工作量。

我们将禁用的第一个功能是对 C 和 C++ 源文件进行更精确的更改跟踪。 Ninja 只是检查文件的修改时间是否已更改，如果更改，则重新编译它。 相比之下，build2 在这种情况下执行额外的步骤：它将（部分预处理的）源文件标记化并计算结果标记的校验和。 如果自上次编译文件以来此校验和没有更改，则它会跳过重新编译它。 这会忽略仅空白的更改（只要它们不更改标记的列号），并且在开发过程中非常有用（并且在某些情况下至关重要，例如如果您想在每次提交时更改项目的版本）。 但是，在从头构建中对所有 299 个翻译单元进行标记会产生前期成本，即使它可能会在进一步的增量构建过程中得到回报。

禁用此可忽略更改检测的方法是告诉 build2 该项目是只读的（这是由包管理器针对外部依赖项自动完成的）。 在这种情况下，build2 将回退到仅使用修改时间，与 Ninja 相同。 通过此更改，我们的构建时间降至 3.4 秒，与 Ninja 的构建时间几乎相同：

Time (mean ± σ):    3.433 s ± 0.055 s  [User: 51.093s, System: 6.701s]
Range (min … max):  3.383 s … 3.551 s  10 runs

让我们看看是否可以走得更快。 接下来，我们禁用文件缓存中的压缩。 稍后我们将更详细地讨论文件缓存，但现在我们只是说，通过禁用压缩，我们可以用临时磁盘空间使用来换取速度：

Time (mean ± σ):    3.355 s ± 0.067 s  [User: 49.987s, System: 6.153s]
Range (min … max):  3.281 s … 3.471 s  10 runs

现在我们比 Ninja 快 2.2%！ 虽然这看起来似乎不多，但考虑到 build2 仍然比 Ninja 做得更多，它就变得更令人印象深刻。 其中一些工作是由 CMake 完成的，有些则根本没有完成。

例如，build2 从 XercesVersion.hpp.in 生成 XercesVersion.hpp 标头作为构建的一部分，而 Ninja 将其留给 CMake。 build2 还确保此文件被正确更改跟踪（而 Ninja 希望您手动重新运行 CMake）。 该标头几乎包含在 Xerces-C++ 中的每个翻译单元中，这意味着在生成它之前无法启动编译。 作为实验，我破解了 build2 构建文件以假装 XercesVersion.hpp 是静态的。 这使得差距扩大至 2.6%。

build2 还必须从编译器中提取更多信息，对于 Ninja 来说，这也是由 CMake 完成的。 诸如编译器 ID（GCC、Clang 等）及其版本、目标平台、系统标头和库搜索路径列表、使用的 C 和 C++ 标准库等之类的信息。这些信息既可用于构建文件，也可用于实现更精确的更改跟踪。 例如，对于 C 和 C++，除了跟踪标准输入（例如源文件本身、所有包含的标头和编译选项）的更改之外，build2 还跟踪编译器 ID/版本、系统标头搜索路径以及可能影响编译的环境变量。

目前，提取此信息的唯一可靠方法是运行编译器。 不幸的是，为了提取上面列出的所有位，我们必须多次运行它。 例如，对于 GCC，总共有 10 次调用，其中 5 次用于 C，5 次用于 C++（Xerces-C++ 有一些 C 翻译单元）：

LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -v
gcc-15 -g -print-multiarch
gcc-15 -g -x c -E -
LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -std=c9x -print-search-dirs
LC_ALL=C gcc-15 -std=c9x -x c -v -E -

LC_ALL=C g++-15 -v
g++-15 -g -print-multiarch
g++-15 -g -x c++ -E -
LC_ALL=C g++-15 -std=gnu++17 -print-search-dirs
LC_ALL=C g++-15 -std=gnu++17 -x c++ -v -E -

好的，所以 build2 做得更多，并且与 Ninja 相当甚至更快，即使我们选择不看大象（CMake）。 下一个自然要问的问题是它是如何做到的？ Ninja 从一开始就考虑到了性能，然后经历了数十年的大量使用和优化。 几乎没有机会让我们采摘任何果实，更不用说那些低垂的果实了。 那么秘密是什么？

简而言之，我们必须以不同的方式做事，而不仅仅是做得更好。 我可以想到促成这一点的三个主要设计决策。 凭经验验证并不容易，因为单独测试替代设计非常困难，但我认为它们是最可能的原因。

第一个更多的是不该做什么，而不是该做什么。 同样，没有什么比上面提到的文章更能说明这一点了：

这是来自另一个开源项目的 CMake 构建的一小部分：

[...]

这里，CMake 使用 xcode-select -print-path 获取 Xcode 的路径，使用 sw_vers 获取操作系统版本，然后递归调用几次 cmake/make 以进行良好的测量，最后编译并链接文件。

只有该时间线中的绿色框在做有用的工作。 有人可能会说，CMake 所做的一切都不是“有用的工作”，因为它只是构建了实际构建项目的东西。 无论如何，让我们接受 CMake 需要执行这种奇怪的 cmake->make->make->clang 舞蹈来确定构建环境。

缩小显示，奇怪的舞蹈发生了 85 次！

哎呀，没有并行性。 它还特意重新检查 Xcode 路径和操作系统版本 85 次，以防操作系统版本在构建过程中发生变化。

不用说，使用这种方法在性能方面不会取得很大的进步。 相比之下，在 build2 中，我们积极缓存每条发现的信息（但不会跨构建系统运行），以确保我们不会重做任何不必要的工作。

好吧，我将不再选择 CMake，而专注于 Ninja。 Ninja 和 build2 之间的第二个最大区别（第一个是它是本机构建系统）是 build2 是多线程的。 虽然 Ninja 并行执行编译器、链接器等，但它从单个线程串行执行自己的内务工作。 例如，Ninja 和 build2 都需要解析从 GCC 接收到的头依赖信息，这些信息不方便地生成为 Makefile 片段。 build2 从多个线程并行执行此操作（以及许多其他操作）。 事实上，build2 中唯一的串行阶段是加载构建文件（即使如此，也有关于如何并行化其中某些部分的想法）。

我认为有助于 build2 匹配或超过 Ninja 速度的最后一个设计决策是在提取标头依赖信息（每个翻译单元包含的标头列表，传递性）时使用不同的 C/C++ 构建模型。

Ninja 使用我们所说的编译模型的副产品：在从头开始构建期间，Ninja 编译每个翻译单元并基本上免费获取标头依赖信息。 它解析它并将其以自己的格式存储在磁盘上，以便在下一次构建期间使用，以查看是否有任何翻译单元需要重新编译，因为它们包含的某些标头可能已更改。 这是一个聪明的方法，但不幸的是它不能很好地与自动生成的标头配合使用（这就是为什么像 XercesVersion.hpp 这样的标头是由 CMake 生成的原因）。

在 build2 中，我们在编译翻译单元之前执行显式标头依赖项提取。 人们可以合理地预期，一种幼稚的实现的性能会比副产品方法更差，因为副产品方法的提取是免费的。 我们在 build2 中所做的有点更高级：因为标头依赖项提取本质上是在翻译单元上运行的预处理器，所以我们将依赖项提取与每个翻译单元的部分预处理结合起来。 或者，换句话说，我们不只是提取标头依赖项，而是对每个翻译单元执行部分预处理（-fdirective-only 对于 GCC，-frewrite-includes 对于 Clang），并获取标头依赖项信息作为其副产品。 然后，当需要编译翻译单元时，我们编译这个部分预处理的输出而不是原始源文件，从而节省了重新预处理的时间。

还记得我们上面禁用的文件缓存压缩吗？ 好吧，该文件缓存是部分预处理的翻译单元的临时缓存（除非使用 C++20 模块）。

不过，这听起来比 Ninja 所做的工作要多得多。 我们甚至必须将部分预处理的文件存储在磁盘上，这怎么能比什么都不做更快呢？ 有趣的是，似乎还有另一个方面在起作用：Ninja 的做法是，翻译单元的预处理按时间分布在整个构建过程中。 由于 C（尤其是 C++）编译是内存密集型的，因此对 RAM 的需求也很大。 相比之下，使用 build2 方法，所有预处理都是前端加载的，全部集中在构建开始时、内存密集型编译开始之前。 典型的 C/C++ 翻译单元的预处理涉及到数百个头文件（其中许多与其他翻译单元相同），所有这些都需要从磁盘读取。 事实证明，至少在使用 GCC 的 Linux 上，build2 方法性能更好，这可能是因为文件访问的时间局部性更好并且内存压力更低。 换句话说，使用 build2 方法，包含的标头更有可能仍然位于系统的文件缓存中（有关详细信息，请参阅单独的预处理和编译性能）。

基准详情

该基准测试是在配备 Intel i9-12900K CPU、在 Samsung 980 Pro NVMe 上运行 Debian、格式化为 ext4 的物理机上执行的。 为了获得稳定的数字，我禁用了睿频加速（失败了，随着 CPU 变暖，时间逐渐增加）：

echo 1 >/sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo

我使用了 Ninja 的官方 Xerces-C++ 3.3.0 源代码存档和 libxerces-c-3.3.0+3 build2 包（这是覆盖了 build2 支持的官方源代码）。 由于 Debian 上的 ICU 系统版本不再支持 C++14，我必须修改 CMakeLists.txt 将硬编码的 C++ 标准从 14 更改为 17。

用于准备 Ninja 构建的 CMake 命令：

CC=gcc-15 CXX=g++-15 cmake -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -Dnetwork:BOOL=OFF \
  -Dtranscoder=icu \
  -Dmessage-loader=inmemory \
  -Dmutex-manager=standard \
  -Dxmlch-type=char16_t \
  ../xerces-c-3.3.0

然后运行 ​​Ninja 基准测试：

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'ninja clean' \
  'ninja src/all'

要运行 build2 基准测试，我们不需要准备任何东西。 以下是上面显示的三个测量的命令行：

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   xercesc/"

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   config.libxerces_c.build.readonly=true xercesc/"

hyperfine --style=basic --warmup 1 --runs 10 \
  --prepare 'b clean: xercesc/' \
  "b --file-cache=none \
   config.c=gcc-15 config.cxx=g++-15 config.cxx.std=gnu++17 \
   config.cc.coptions=-g config.bin.lib=shared \
   config.libxerces_c.build.readonly=true xercesc/"
